nameStory: Common Lionspaw gets its dramatic name from its fuzzy, orange flower clusters that supposedly resemble a lion's paw - though you might need to squint a bit to see it! The scientific name Leonotis literally means 'lion's ear,' which is why it's also called lion's ear in many places. Both names celebrate the bold, shaggy appearance of those distinctive flower heads.
description: Common Lionspaw is a striking evergreen shrub from South Africa that's built like a member of the mint family - because it is one! It grows as a tall, upright plant with square stems and can reach 4-6 feet in height. The most eye-catching feature is its rings of bright orange, tubular flowers that encircle the stems at regular intervals, creating a dramatic tiered effect. With its soft, grayish-green leaves and bold architecture, it's definitely a showstopper in any garden where it can survive our winters.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright orange, tubular flowers arranged in dense, fuzzy whorls that completely encircle the stem at regular intervals, creating a distinctive tiered or layered look up the plant

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, grayish-green leaves arranged in opposite pairs along square stems - run your finger along the stem and you'll feel those telltale mint family edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright shrub growing 4-6 feet high with a somewhat open, architectural structure that makes those flower rings really stand out

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel sturdy and slightly fuzzy to the touch - a classic mint family trait that you can confirm by rolling the stem between your fingers

idTips.label: Overall Texture
idTips.description: The whole plant has a soft, velvety feel when you brush against it, from the fuzzy flower clusters to the slightly downy leaves

habitat: In New England, you'll only find Common Lionspaw as a cultivated garden plant, typically in protected spots or containers that can be moved indoors for winter. It thrives in well-drained soil and full sun locations, often planted in herb gardens or decorative borders. Since it's native to South Africa, it can't survive our harsh New England winters outdoors and is usually treated as an annual or brought inside.

seasonality.spring: If grown as a houseplant brought outdoors, new growth emerges with fresh, soft leaves on square stems. Container plants moved outside after frost danger show vigorous growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with those spectacular orange flower whorls appearing in tiers up the stems. The plant reaches its full dramatic height and architectural beauty.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in warm years, but growth slows as temperatures drop. Time to plan for bringing container plants indoors.
seasonality.winter: Only survives indoors in New England - outdoor plants are killed by frost. Indoor plants may go dormant or continue growing slowly in bright windows.

funFact: This plant is sometimes called 'wild dagga' in its native South Africa, where 'dagga' comes from an ancient Khoikhoi word - but it's completely unrelated to cannabis despite the nickname, and the 'wild' part helps distinguish it from the stuff that shares the same slang term!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded sighting in New England, confusion is unlikely, but its orange tubular flowers might remind you of native cardinal flower - except cardinal flower is bright red, loves wet feet, and has a completely different leaf arrangement. Think 'orange rings around square stems' for lionspaw versus 'red spikes above wet ground' for cardinal flower.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wild dagga,' this plant has nothing to do with cannabis - it's just a case of shared slang terms in South African culture. The name can confuse gardeners who might worry about what they're actually growing, but it's simply a member of the mint family with no legal concerns.
compareHints: Since Common Lionspaw is the only Leonotis species recorded in New England, compare it to other mint family members like bee balm or salvia. Unlike the scattered flower heads of bee balm, lionspaw's flowers form complete rings around the stem. Unlike most salvias with their blue or purple spikes, lionspaw creates orange whorls that stack up the stem like nature's own apartment building.
